title: Dubai Passenger Caught Hiding Gold Capsules in Mouth at Bengaluru Airport
excerpt: CISF personnel intercepted an Indian national at Kempegowda International Airport after discovering two yellow-metal capsules weighing 82 grams concealed in his oral cavity during a routine security screening.
body:
• CISF personnel at Bengaluru's Kempegowda International Airport found two gold capsules weighing approximately 82 grams concealed inside a passenger's mouth during a pre-embarkation security check.
  • The passenger, identified as Mohd Siraj, had arrived from Dubai on IndiGo flight 6E-1486 and was headed to Ghaziabad on a connecting domestic flight.
  • This is the second gold smuggling interception at KIA within a week — on August 20, two mules carrying 260 grams of gold powder in customized trousers were caught after arriving from Bangkok.
  • The passenger has been handed over to KIA police for further investigation and legal action.

Suspicious Behavior Triggers Discovery

Central Industrial Security Force personnel at Kempegowda International Airport in Bengaluru intercepted a passenger on Tuesday after detecting two yellow-metal capsules concealed inside his mouth during a routine security screening.

The passenger, identified as Mohd Siraj, an Indian national, had arrived at Terminal 1 aboard IndiGo flight 6E-1486 from Dubai at around 4:17 AM on August 26. He was scheduled to board a connecting domestic flight to Ghaziabad on IndiGo flight 6E-2518, departing at 9:20 AM, according to CISF officials.

During the pre-embarkation security check at a frisking point in Terminal 1, CISF Sub-Inspector Deepak Kumar Sharma noticed that Siraj was not responding appropriately to the screening officer and was acting unnaturally during verbal questioning. Sharma flagged the passenger and alerted the concerned officer for a more thorough examination.

"The passenger thought the body scanner would not go over his shoulder and that it would be best to place them in his mouth during screening."

— CISF sources

82 Grams of Gold Recovered

Upon further physical examination, security officers discovered two metallic capsules concealed inside Siraj's oral cavity. The capsules weighed approximately 82 grams in total. Sources said the passenger believed he could bypass the body scanners by hiding the gold in his mouth, banking on the assumption that the scanner would not cover that area.

The nature and precise value of the recovered yellow metal have not yet been officially ascertained, though at current market rates, 82 grams of gold would be worth approximately ₹6.5 lakh. CISF personnel handed Siraj over to KIA police for further legal action, and an investigation is underway to determine the intended destination of the concealed material.

Second Interception in a Week

The incident marks the second gold smuggling interception at Kempegowda International Airport within the span of a week, both carried out under the CISF unit led by DIG and CASO Manjunath H.

On August 20, CISF personnel apprehended two mules carrying 260 grams of gold in powder form concealed in customized trousers. The two passengers had arrived from Bangkok and were flagged after security personnel observed unusual behavior during screening. Both were handed over to police for questioning.

A Persistent Challenge on India-Gulf Routes

Gold smuggling through Indian airports remains a persistent challenge for security agencies. Bengaluru's Kempegowda International Airport, which handles a high volume of flights connecting India to the Gulf region, has been a frequent point of interception. Smugglers have employed increasingly creative methods to avoid detection — from gold paste in capsules and powder hidden in clothing to precious metal concealed inside pasta-making machines and electronic devices.

In June 2026, customs officials at the same airport seized gold worth ₹1.37 crore from a Dubai passenger who had hidden gold paste inside four capsules. The continued interceptions suggest that the Dubai-Bengaluru corridor remains one of the most active smuggling routes, despite stepped-up vigilance by both CISF and customs authorities.

For NRI travelers on India-Gulf routes, the heightened security means longer screening times and more rigorous checks, particularly on flights arriving from Dubai, Sharjah, and other Gulf cities known as gold smuggling origin points.
